schools.summary: Gill notes only the tribe’s name and its first king, and contrasts this Saul with the apostle of the same tribe.
Keil and Delitzsch read the genealogy as a signal of Saul’s coming importance and reconcile it with Chronicles by omitted links; Ellicott explains the discrepancies as editorial pruning.
Henry takes the three senses of the father’s “power” together and dwells on Benjamin’s smallness and dignity.
Clarke renders the phrase literally and jokes that strength was the only power Kish had.

debates.question: How is Kish’s descent to be squared with the Chronicles line?

sides.position: Kish is son of Abiel, and Ner in Chronicles is grandfather or remoter ancestor, links being passed over
Ner stands between Abiel and Kish, and each summary omits names not needed for its purpose

debates.question: What does “a mighty man of power” describe?

sides.position: A man of property, not a brave man
Literally a strong man, and that was the only power he had
All three at once: bold in spirit, strong in body, wealthy in estate
A noble and opulent Benjamite of Gibeah

outliers.note: He reports Dean Payne Smith’s view that the civil war after the crime at Gibeah destroyed many older Benjamite records, which is partly why the genealogies tangle.

themes: the tribe of Benjamin after the war of Gibeah
a root out of dry ground
1.pericope_label: Kish the Benjamite and his lineage

schools.summary: Gill marks the contrast with the later Saul of the same tribe, a little man where this one was tall.
Ellicott argues the first epithet cannot mean both choice and young and settles on “a young man”; Keil and Delitzsch run the description straight into the errand.
Henry reads the description for what it omits, and sets a king after God’s heart against a king after the people’s.
Clarke and Wesley both explain the stature from ancient and eastern valuation of a tall king.

debates.question: Can the first epithet mean both “choice” and “young”?

sides.position: No: one Hebrew word cannot carry both, and the translators followed the Latin electus; “a young man” is best, Saul being about forty to forty-five
The English pairing is left standing and the stature alone is explained

debates.question: Why is Saul’s height recorded?

sides.position: Because elective kingship paid great respect to personal appearance
Because tall stature was much valued in a king in the east
Because heroic proportions were prized in the childhood of nations, and helped Israel accept him
To show that nothing but size was on offer, no wisdom, virtue, learning or piety

outliers.note: He notes that Saul did not even excel in strength as he did in height: Israel slighted Samson and is justly put off with a tall man weak as other men.

themes: higher than any of the people from his shoulders upward
a king after the people’s heart
2.pericope_label: Saul, a choice young man, head and shoulders above the people

schools.summary: Gill states the loss plainly, the animals having strayed from stable or field.
Henry turns the errand into lessons on diligence, obedience and the loss of property, and reads the smallness of the occasion as design.
Clarke explains the value of asses in a land without horses and marvels at the chain of events; Wesley adds that the search was not beneath Saul in those simpler times.
Ellicott reads the Hebrew as she-asses kept for breeding, gives the legal ground of the scarcity of horses, and defends the servant’s standing in the house.

debates.question: Is the chain of small events chance or design?

sides.position: Everything goes on in the common course, yet all conspired to favour an election God did not approve
The smallness is the design: Saul stepped at once from the level of his neighbours to the throne, as Hannah sang

outliers.note: He supposes there was no way to give public notice of strayed asses, and suspects the law obliging a man to return his neighbour’s beast was neglected like other good ones.

themes: asses in a land without horses
3.pericope_label: The asses of Kish are lost

schools.summary: Gill reads Mount Ephraim as the part next Benjamin and identifies Zuph by Samuel’s birthplace, citing the Targum.
Ellicott gives etymologies and locations for Shalisha, Shalim and Zuph; Keil and Delitzsch give the textual reason Saul turned back.
Henry pairs the failed errand with the kingdom found, and turns the father’s fear into a charge to children.
Clarke sets out Calmet’s route and then withdraws confidence in it, the places being unknown.

debates.question: Can the route of the search be traced?

sides.position: Calmet’s circuit of some twenty-five leagues can be set out, but we do not know where the places were, and the Targum gives quite different names
The regions can be identified from their names and from the lie of the hill country

outliers.note: He quotes Dr Kitto’s verdict that Saul’s regard for his father’s feelings here is a favourable indication of character.

themes: he missed what he sought and met a kingdom
4.pericope_label: The circuit of the search, and the servant consulted

schools.summary: Gill is careful that the proposal came from the servant, not from Saul.
Keil and Delitzsch catch the gesture in “in this city”; Ellicott reads the servant’s simplicity as evidence of how Samuel was loved in the countryside.
Henry calls it a poor business to employ a prophet about, and contrasts asking one’s fortune with asking one’s duty.
Wesley hears doubt in the “peradventure” about whether God would answer on so mean a matter.

debates.question: Does the servant’s proposal do him credit?

sides.position: Yes: that he thought such a loss warranted intruding on the prophet-judge says much for Samuel’s kindly name even in secluded farms
He spoke very respectfully of a man he knew only by common fame
He doubted whether so great a prophet would be granted a revelation about such mean matters
The use proposed for the man of God was poor: better to have given the asses up and gone to learn the knowledge of God

outliers.note: He draws from the mere accident of their position that many will consult a man of God who comes in their way but would not go a step out of their way for wisdom.

themes: a man of God, an honourable man
all that he saith cometh surely to pass
6.pericope_label: There is in this city a man of God

schools.summary: Gill follows the Targum’s “if he receives money” and finds Saul uncertain whether Samuel took such things at all.
Keil and Delitzsch let the servant’s quarter shekel remove the obstacle Saul raised; Ellicott calls the gift respectful homage rather than a fee and supplies parallels.
Clarke denies the prophets took money and grounds the present in the eastern custom of never approaching a superior empty-handed; Wesley multiplies its possible purposes.

debates.question: What did a present to a prophet signify?

sides.position: Not a fee for prediction, but the invariable custom of never approaching a superior empty-handed
An act of respectful homage in many cases, like Jacob’s spicery or the Queen of Sheba’s gifts
Any of several things: respect, grateful acknowledgement, the support of the prophets, or relief of the needy known to them
Saul could not tell whether Samuel accepted such things at all, having no knowledge of him

outliers.note: He supports the custom from Ward’s account of Bengal, where a petitioner brings fruits or sweetmeats and is greatly wounded if the gift is refused.

themes: what shall we bring the man?
7.pericope_label: What shall we bring the man?

schools.summary: Henry weighs and rejects the harsh reading, defends the propriety of the gift, and keeps one sting for Saul.
Clarke reckons the quarter shekel at about ninepence and calls it a token of respect, not an emolument.
Ellicott declines the calculation and quotes Dean Payne Smith on a roughly stamped shekel divided by a cross.

debates.question: Did Saul’s small fee measure Samuel by the false prophets?

sides.position: Some think so, coming to him as to a fortune-teller and reckoning a quarter shekel enough
Rather it agreed with the usage of the times and natural equity, and little as it was it was the widow’s mite

outliers.note: He notes that Saul raised the want of a present as an objection to going at all, not owning that he had money, and remarks that most people love a cheap religion.

themes: the fourth part of a shekel
8.pericope_label: The fourth part of a shekel of silver

schools.summary: Gill reads inquiring of God, with the Targum, as asking doctrine of him through a man eminent for grace and prophecy.
Keil and Delitzsch call it a notice introduced to light what follows; Ellicott traces the history of “seer” and insists the inserter was a reviser of high authority.
Henry turns the title on those who would hold the office: prophets must first be seers.
Clarke denies the verse was originally part of the book and distinguishes seer from prophet at length; Wesley leaves Samuel’s own authorship open.

debates.question: Whose hand wrote this parenthesis?

sides.position: Not the original author: it fits the theory of later compilation from memoranda, and reads better after the eleventh verse
A later hand, perhaps in Ezra’s time, but a reviser of very high authority
Either a later sacred writer or Samuel himself, old enough to say “beforetime” of his own first days
Simply a notice the historian introduces to throw light on what follows

debates.question: How do “seer” and “prophet” differ?

sides.position: The seer was always a prophet, but the prophet not always a seer: the seer saw symbolical representations of God
Seer was the oldest of the three titles and decayed in meaning, while prophet came into common use in Samuel’s day
The title names a function: he discerned and could discover things secret

outliers.note: He offers Virgil’s Sibyl as a specimen of the diviner’s boast of sight, professing herself a seer of wars and of a river foaming with blood.

themes: a later hand in the text
9.pericope_label: The parenthesis about seers and prophets

schools.summary: Gill renders the assent “good is thy word”, derives Ramah’s name from its height, and reads Saul’s hope for the asses.
Keil and Delitzsch insist the word means the high place of sacrifice, not a hill; Ellicott builds a four-point case that the city was Ramah.
Henry values the maidens’ helpfulness and finds it remarkable that Saul had never seen Samuel.
Clarke takes the women at the well as evidence against the notion that young women were kept shut up at home.

debates.question: What is “the hill” they went up to?

sides.position: Not a height generally but the high place as a place of sacrifice or prayer
The hill the city was built on, whence its name Ramah, signifying high and lifted up

outliers.note: He allows one advantage in Saul’s ignorance of Samuel, that no secret compact between them could be suspected, but refuses to call it any commendation.

themes: the high place and the hill
10.pericope_label: They went to the city, and met maidens drawing water

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the plain sense and infers from the promptness that Samuel’s house stood near the gate they entered.
Ellicott hears an eye-witness in the maidens’ eager reply; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the blessing as the thanksgiving prayer before the meal and the opening word as “immediately”.
Henry explains the high place as an irregularity the times allowed, the tabernacle having lost the ark.
Clarke places Samuel’s other dwelling at Naioth and describes the feast; Wesley has him returning from travels and divides the blessing in two.

debates.question: Where had Samuel come from that day?

sides.position: From his country dwelling at Naioth, where there was probably a school of the prophets
From travels abroad, returning to his own house in Ramah
Either from his circuit or from his country seat; his movements were generally known

debates.question: What is Samuel’s blessing of the sacrifice?

sides.position: The thanksgiving prayer customarily offered before the sacrificial meal
Thanksgiving for a thank-offering, and prayer for its acceptance
A matter of office: he alone could perform the rites used on the occasion
A very early instance of the devout Hebrew practice of asking a blessing on meals

outliers.note: He offers a living parallel from the Arabs, who make a large feast of sacrificed camels and invite the neighbourhood, as in the bidding of guests here.

themes: he came today to the city
the sacrifice in the high place
make haste, for he will come
12.pericope_label: He is before you: make haste, for he comes today

schools.summary: Gill has the two go up the hill to the city of Ramah.

Keil and Delitzsch set the meeting at the gate, mark the historian’s break to the previous day, and gloss the opening of the ear and the sending; Ellicott frames the encounter with a long passage from Ewald.

debates.question: Does the promise of saving Israel from the Philistines contradict the earlier account of their subjection?

sides.position: No: the earlier account asserts only that there was no longer any permanent oppression

outliers.note: He borrows Ewald’s reading of the scene as a study in unconsciousness, Saul bashfully pursuing his humble quest while a portion higher than other men’s had long been reserved for him by heaven.

themes: Samuel came out to meet them
the LORD had opened Samuel’s ear
I will send thee a man
two kinds of ignorance at the gate
14.pericope_label: They came into the city, and Samuel came out to meet them

schools.summary: Gill keeps the whispering picture without the archaeology and reads the promise as a study in unconscious providence.

Ellicott explains the idiom from pushing aside the head-dress and makes the Philistine raids the immediate cause of the demand for a king; Keil and Delitzsch meet the same difficulty on textual ground.
Clarke declines to say how the communication was made and insists the word is captain, not king; Wesley puts the Ammonites in the foreground and the Philistines in the fear.

debates.question: How was the revelation made to Samuel?

sides.position: Literally, the LORD uncovered his ear: the image is of pushing aside the head-dress to whisper
A private manner, a whispering in the ear, as a secret told in a friendly way
Secret, perhaps by a still small voice
How it was made we cannot tell

debates.question: Which enemy prompted the request for a king?

sides.position: The Philistines, again harassing Israelite territory with destructive raids
The Ammonites pressed them at that moment, but the Philistines were the constant and most dreaded enemy

outliers.note: He produces Alexander’s judgement that the truest line in the Iliad was the one calling Atrides great in the war and great in acts of sway, to show that no king was esteemed who was not a warrior.

themes: the cry of the people has come unto me
which enemy drove the demand for a king
15.pericope_label: The LORD had told Samuel in his ear the day before

schools.summary: Gill has Samuel notice the stranger’s height and fix his eyes on him, wanting to be left in no uncertainty.
Ellicott makes the question an explicit silent prayer and renders the closing verb “shall control” or “shall restrain”; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the same verb as coercing a people by authority.
Clarke draws a conclusion about the man rather than the moment, on Samuel’s constant familiarity with God.

debates.question: What does the closing verb say about Saul’s reign?

sides.position: Not “shall reign” but “shall control” or “shall restrain”, a stern, severe rule, looking forward to what the reign became
The Latin sense of coercing a people by authority

outliers.note: He turns from the exchange to the man, marvelling at the intimate communion and constant familiarity that seems to have existed between Samuel and his God.

themes: the tacit inquiry, is this he?
he shall reign over my people
a stern rule foretold at the outset
17.pericope_label: Behold the man whom I spake to thee of

schools.summary: Gill leaves the location open between Samuel’s own door and the city gate.
Keil and Delitzsch defend “in the gate” against Thenius; Ellicott thinks the Greek “in the midst of the city” may be original.
Henry fastens on the irony and builds a portrait of Samuel’s plainness out of it.

debates.question: Where did Saul come up with Samuel?

sides.position: In the gate: the phrase specifies the general statement that they entered the city, and Thenius’s alteration is unnecessary
Possibly in the midst of the city, as the Greek reads, a scribe easily writing gate for city
Either at the door of Samuel’s own house or within the gate as Saul entered

outliers.note: He notes that Samuel took no state upon him, had no attendants or ensigns of honour or distinguishing habit, so that Saul took him for a porter rather than a prophet.

themes: in the gate or in the midst of the city
great worth under a despicable appearance
18.pericope_label: Tell me, where is the seer's house?

schools.summary: Gill is careful that “I am the seer” was said for information’s sake, not in pride.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the shift from singular to plural as an express invitation to the servant, and refuse to read “all that is in thine heart” as all that troubles him; Ellicott follows both points.
Henry turns the answer into a parable of being known before knowing, and reads the detention as pastoral management.
Clarke reads the declaration forward, as preparing Saul for what was to follow.

debates.question: Why was Saul told to go up first?

sides.position: Letting a person go ahead was a sign of great esteem
A mark of distinguished honour from one of Samuel’s rank to a young unknown wayfarer
Perhaps simply because business obliged Samuel to call somewhere on the way

debates.question: What does “all that is in thine heart” mean?

sides.position: Not what lies heavy on it, since the asses are dealt with at once, but the thoughts of his heart generally, told to prove Samuel a prophet
His secret thoughts and aspirations, the asses being dismissed from his mind altogether

outliers.note: He reads the whole detention as management of a soul: Saul had nothing in his mind but his father’s asses, and Samuel meant to take him off that care — let us pray together, and then we will talk together.

themes: all that is in thine heart
tomorrow I will let thee go
19.pericope_label: I am the seer: go up before me to the high place

schools.summary: Gill reports Kimchi and the Targum on the three days and stresses the convincing exactness of the telling.
Henry supplies the compliment buried in the question and reads Saul’s answer as modesty that presaged preferment.
Clarke calls the speech exceedingly modest and asks who can bear prosperity; Wesley extends the promise to Saul’s posterity.
Ellicott denies that the phrase means what Israel desires and reads the dark words as meant to lift Saul above small matters.

debates.question: What is “all the desire of Israel”?

sides.position: The thing Israel desires, namely a king
Not what Israel desires but all it possesses of what is precious, as the Latin and Luther render it

debates.question: Is Saul’s protest about his tribe modesty or fact?

sides.position: Modesty, and a good presage of preferment; he probably supposed Samuel was bantering him
Historical fact: the tribe was cut to six hundred men and never recovered, and was afterwards reckoned with Judah

outliers.note: He extends the promise past Saul himself to his family or posterity after his death, if by his sin he does not cut off the entail.

20.pericope_label: The asses are found, and Saul protests his tribe

schools.summary: Gill calls the room simply the dining room of the house belonging to the high place.

Ellicott calls “parlour” an unfortunate rendering, reads Samuel’s silence as deliberate, and finds the whole feast arranged beforehand; Keil and Delitzsch explain the servant’s place and the thirty guests.
Henry draws out what the honour cost the host, Saul’s advancement being Samuel’s own deposing.
Clarke attends to the cook, whose title comes from a root meaning to slay; Wesley reads the chief seat as public preparation.

debates.question: Why was Saul given the chief seat?

sides.position: To raise the company’s expectation and ready them to pay him the honour his approaching dignity required
To awaken new and grander thoughts in him, Samuel answering his protest with no word but this
In compliance with the will of God, though Saul’s advancement was Samuel’s own deposing

outliers.note: He notes the tradition that the servant was Doeg the Edomite, who would then have had here a foretaste of the rank he later held among Saul’s officers of state.

themes: the parlour or cell at the high place
22.pericope_label: The parlour, the thirty persons, and the reserved portion

schools.summary: Gill lists the candidates for what was served with the shoulder and argues that Samuel, though a Levite, might officiate as priest and so dispose of the right shoulder.
Keil and Delitzsch reject Dathe, Maurer and Thenius and follow Luther; Ellicott quotes Dean Payne Smith to make the cook, not Samuel, the speaker.
Henry makes the left shoulder Samuel’s own portion, so that giving it away resigned his place, and reads shoulder and breast as strength and affection.
Clarke guesses at the caul and the fore-quarter and makes the shoulder an emblem of government; Wesley takes the closing words for Samuel’s.

debates.question: What was served with the shoulder?

sides.position: Not broth and not the kidney, but, with Luther, the fat attached to the leg that was not destined for the altar
A sauce or garnish, or the thigh with the Targum and Jarchi and Kimchi, or on older Jewish authority the breast
Part of the caul, to roast the better; the Targum gives the fore-leg down to the knee, perhaps the whole fore-quarter

debates.question: Which shoulder was set before Saul, and why?

sides.position: Earlier commentators said the left, the right falling to the priests
The right, Samuel officiating as priest, which best accounts for his disposal of it
The left, Samuel’s own portion at the upper end of the table, so that the gift resigned his place
Whichever it was, it was chosen as an emblem of the government now laid on him, not as the best part

debates.question: Who speaks the closing words?

sides.position: Samuel, explaining that he had bidden the cook reserve this part for Saul
The cook: Samuel’s name is not in the Hebrew, and the Syriac and Chaldee agree with it against the Greek and Latin
holders: Dean Payne Smith (as quoted by Ellicott)

outliers.note: He passes on Payne Smith’s remark that the chat of the cook is entirely after the manner of ancient times, and would show Saul how completely his coming had been foreseen.

themes: the shoulder and that which was upon it

schools.summary: Gill solves the descent from the high place two ways and reports Abarbinel on the sleepless night.
Keil and Delitzsch deny the conversation can have turned on the kingdom; Ellicott follows Otto von Gerlach in supplying its subject and judges the Greek reading a correction.
Henry fills the evening conversation out at length, with Samuel satisfying Saul and offering to resign.
Clarke explains the flat roofs of the East as places for walking, talking and sleeping; Wesley says the talk concerned the kingdom.

debates.question: What was the subject of the evening conversation?

sides.position: The kingdom designed for Saul by God
The whole story of the people’s desire of a king, with assurance that Saul was the man and that Samuel would willingly resign
Not the royal call, which was not made known as a word of Jehovah until the next day: the talk was meant to prepare him for it
The religious and political decline of Israel, the heathen opposition, and the need of an obedient leader

debates.question: Why does the Greek read that a couch was strewn for Saul?

sides.position: Apparently a correction, the translators being unable to understand an evening conversation before so formal an announcement next morning

outliers.note: He lets the question that provoked the Greek alteration stand unanswered: why did Samuel not tell Saul of God’s intention during that evening spent together?

themes: the flat roof as a place of private conversation
the Greek couch for the Hebrew communing
25.pericope_label: Samuel communes with Saul upon the top of the house

schools.summary: Gill reports Abarbinel’s supposition that neither man could sleep, and what kept each awake.
Ellicott calls the English of the verse misleading and restores the Hebrew order; Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way and locate the two voices.
Clarke makes the point briskly: Saul had slept on the roof all night, so there was no calling him up a second time.

debates.question: Did either man sleep that night?

sides.position: Neither could, on Abarbinel’s supposition: Samuel for thinking of the anointing, Saul for the hint and the honour
Saul slept soundly, probably heavily, weary after the day’s scene and revelations

debates.question: How should the summons be rendered?

sides.position: Get up, that I may send thee
Get up, I will conduct thee

outliers.note: He makes the escort the reason for the early call: Samuel wished to conduct Saul himself out of the city, having a yet more important communication to make.

themes: about the spring of the day
Samuel called from below to the roof
up, that I may send thee away
26.pericope_label: They arose early, and Samuel called Saul from the roof

schools.summary: Gill gives the topography, the city on a hill and its end a descent toward Saul’s road home.
Ellicott presses the question of Saul’s state of mind and notes the writer’s silence; Keil and Delitzsch give the wording of the command only.
Clarke reads the prompt obedience and glosses the word of God as the counsel or design of the LORD; Wesley gives Samuel’s reason for the secrecy.

debates.question: Why was the servant sent on ahead?

sides.position: So that they might speak privately of the kingdom, which Samuel concealed lest he be thought to impose a king, and so that the lot might show the choice was God’s destination and not Samuel’s contrivance
So that the prophet might in all solemn confidence impart the word of God

outliers.note: He supplies a principle in place of the missing report of Saul’s state of mind: when new duties are imposed by God, He never forgets to bestow the gift of new powers.

themes: down to the end of the city
27.pericope_label: Stand thou still, that I may shew thee the word of God
